articleTitle: Observations of colloidal states using ultrasound velocity measurements
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Ultrasound in the Process Industry
abstract: The following systems are discussed from the point of view of the utilisation of ultrasound velocity scanning to understand the behaviour of concentrated colloidal systems: the sedimentation behaviour of well defined monodisperse silica latex particles in a non-aqueous continuous phase, where long range repulsive interactions result in ordering in the sediment and formation of a colloidal crystal state; and the sedimentation and consolidation behaviour of a concentrated industrial suspension of organic particulates in both the stable and the flocculated state.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Flare gas metering and high pressure gas metering using ultrasonic sensors
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Ultrasound in the Process Industry
abstract: Ultrasonic gas flowmeters are, a new development because of the difficulties due to the low acoustic coupling between an ultrasonic transducer and the gas. This problem has now been reduced by more efficient transducers, better acoustic matching and more efficient electronics for signal analysis. This development has resulted in gradually exchange from hot wire flowmeters to acoustic flowmeters for flare gas measurement in the oil and gas industry. The same process has now been initiated concerning use of multibeam high precision ultrasonic gas flowmeters instead of the traditional differential pressure flowmeters and turbine meters.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of acoustic pyrometry to gas temperature measurement and mapping
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Ultrasound in the Process Industry
abstract: CODEL have developed a system which allows accurate temperature measurement, reliably and continuously, with the facility to produce high resolution temperature maps. This process, which is rugged and non-contact, is known as acoustic pyrometry. A detailed study of the internal temperature profiles can give a previously unseen picture of the inside of the operating furnace. Acoustic pyrometry uses the velocity of sound in the gases within the furnace to calculate the temperature. By using an array of acoustic transducers placed around the enclosure, mean temperatures along a variety of paths can be determined and from that data a temperature profile map computed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Ultrasound in the Process Industry
abstract: Cross correlation transit-time measuring instrumentation can be accurate to a few parts per million depending upon the sensing technology. When ultrasonic sensors are used to measure fluid flow the accuracy is primarily determined by the fluid properties and flow profile. In multiphase mixtures, very large changes of acoustic attenuation can occur and this originally provided the impetus to produce the ultrasonic cross-correlation flowmeter. In its basic form the instrument measures the flow velocity by determining the transit time of changes of acoustic impedance, due to flow disturbances, between two parallel ultrasonic beams spaced a known distance apart. Since only the transit time is measured between two fixed marker beams, the measurement is largely unaffected by wide variations in the speed of sound in the fluid and the fluid properties. The correlation signal processor used in all trials reported in this paper was a commercially available instrument specifically designed for accurate transit time determination and velocity tracking and is based on a multichannel design system. The measurable transit time range was from 0.5 ms to 400 ms corresponding to a velocity range of 0.1 m/s to 80 m/s for a sensor spacing of 40 mm. This instrument can also process phase and amplitude modulation data simultaneously so that fluids varying from single phase to multiphase can be metered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Real-time ultrasound process tomography in pipelines
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Ultrasound in the Process Industry
abstract: The primary descriptor of the interaction of ultrasound with a material is its acoustic impedance. This is related closely to density and hence variations in density can be sensed, e.g. a piped liquid containing gas bubbles. The greater the difference in acoustic impedance at the interface, the greater will be the amount of energy reflected. Conversely if the impedances are similar most of the energy is transmitted. Reflections may provide a basis for process tomography where the materials of interest have distinctly different acoustic impedance values; water and air, for example, fulfil this requirement. The complete interaction behaviour is complex and depends not simply upon the differences in acoustic impedance, but on the size and shape of the interface. These various interactions lead to three basic modes of ultrasound tomography: transmission mode; reflection mode; and diffraction mode.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Ultrasound in the Process Industry
abstract: There has been an increasing demand in industrial flow measurement for the measurement of the mass flowrate of fluids (liquids or gases) rather than their volumetric flowrate. This has been particularly true for fluids where the energy flow is related to the mass flowrate of the fluid rather than its volumetric flowrate. The use of ultrasonic techniques for the mass flowrate measurement of liquids provides a technique which is non-intrusive and can be employed over the whole range of pipe sizes encountered in industrial situations. The authors discuss the mass flow measurement method based on an acoustic impedance measurement system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Sonochemistry in industry, progress and prospects
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Ultrasound in the Process Industry
abstract: In sonochemistry the effects of high power ultrasound in liquids are harnessed for chemical benefit. Apart from streaming, which induces local mixing in the process medium, the main sonophysical effect is cavitation, which not only enhances local mass transfer, but brings about mechanical damage at solid-liquid interfaces, localised extremes of temperature and pressure (the 'hot-spot' mechanism), and transient electrical effects. Depending upon the process in question, these effects manifest themselves in increased reaction rate, easier initiation, less extreme process conditions and changes in reaction path or selectivity. For some technologists, perhaps less familiar with recent advances, there remain, some questions regarding the usefulness of ultrasound to developing processes and the feasibility of using the technique at scale in demanding industrial environments. It is these two questions which are addressed in the paper.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Ultrasound in the Process Industry
abstract: This paper reports on some of the work currently being undertaken at Cranfield University on the application of ultrasound scanning technology for imaging two-phase flows. In particular, a discussion is provided on the type of images that have been obtained from a B-scan using a linear phases array operating at 7.5 MHz. Examples of the range of images that have been obtained using this technology are provided and methods of processing them to infer some of the characteristics of two-phase flows are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Ultrasound in the Process Industry
abstract: The authors have developed a novel wide bandwidth ultrasonic spectrometer for the study of flocculation processes in colloidal systems. The instrument measures the ultrasonic compression wave absorption coefficient and phase velocity as functions of frequency between 1 MHz and 60 MHz, and has a measurement time of less than 100 ms, depending on the signal to noise conditions. The high speed of operation implies that the instrument can be used to study systems undergoing chemical reaction, ordering phenomena such as flocculation, and other physical changes. The authors summarise the measurement technique, ultrasonic wave propagation in colloidal systems, and their preliminary experiments on stable and unstable colloids.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
